sweep_summary: Spanish (stan1288), catalog 'lexical' on Navarro Tomás 1918 with Gibson 2011 secondary. 173 title hits: 9 open texts downloaded and read this search of works with stress in the title (Oltra-Massuet & Arregi 2005, Baković 2016, Hualde 2007, Hualde 2010, Aske 1990 [scanned], Martínez-Paricio 2013, Llisterri et al. 2003, Schwab & Llisterri 2012, Gibson 2011) plus Fuchs 2018 already held by the project. Every first-hand statement read agrees: one contrastive primary stress per word within a right-edge three-syllable window, with ending-conditioned defaults (V-final penult, C-final final; verbs morphologically fixed) and lexically listed exceptions; secondary stress is non-contrastive and postlexical (Hualde 2007, 2010), which refines the catalog's the secondary-stress rule rather than contradicting it. No source contradicts the classification; none supersedes Navarro Tomás as deciding source (Baković 2016 is the clearest modern open statement). About 55 items are word-stress relevant, the rest intonation/focus/rhythm/L2 or false hits (Torres 2003 psychological stress, Raynor 2024 'foot'). new_statements.quote: Stress in vowel-final non-verbs in Spanish regularly falls on the penultimate syllable, while stress in consonant-final words regularly falls on the final syllable. There are two main classes of exceptions to this regularity: stress on the syllable preceding the regular one, and stress on the syllable following the regular one. ... A third class of exceptions consists of a handful of relatively uncommon words (e.g. régimen, espécimen, ínterin) ... that distinguish themselves further by ending in a consonant but having antepenultimate stress.
new_statements.citation: Baković, Eric. 2016. Exceptionality in Spanish stress. Catalan Journal of Linguistics 15: 9-25. doi:10.5565/rev/catjl.182 (open access)
new_statements.reading: Non-verb stress has an ending-conditioned regular pattern (V-final penult, C-final final) with lexically listed exception classes on either side (sábana, caníbal; Panamá) and a tiny C-final antepenult class; i.e. stress is lexically specified within a right-edge three-syllable window with defaults — the same reading as the catalog's 'lexical'. Corroborated in this search of works with stress in the title by Oltra-Massuet & Arregi 2005 ((41): same generalizations, recast as 'stress on the vowel preceding the theme'), Aske 1990 (~95% predictable from final segment, ~4-5% lexical exceptions), Martínez-Paricio 2013 and Hualde 2007 (content words always stressed on one of the last three syllables; secondary stress non-contrastive and postlexical).

new_statements.quote: Unlike Catalan, there is no phonological vowel reduction in Castilian Spanish. Speakers produce the same five vocalic phonemes in stressed and unstressed positions. Therefore, the vowel qualities of [i] and [o] in the verb endings –mino and –minó (or –nimo and –nimó) will remain unchanged regardless of their bearing a stress or not. Consequently, determino and determinó will be true minimal pairs in Castilian Spanish because they only contrast in stress and not in vowel quality. [p. 32:] These results, together with those of previous literature of Catalan and Spanish, provide experimental evidence that the trading between F0 and other stress correlates which characterizes stress accent languages takes place in Catalan and Spanish as well.

new_statements.translation: § 9.1g: In Spanish the position of the stress is partially free, since it can only fall on one of the last three syllables of the word, counting from its right edge. In phonological studies this property is called the THREE-SYLLABLE WINDOW. [...] § 9.4a: Normally, words ending in a vowel are paroxytone (cambio, clase, delante, mala), while those ending in a consonant are usually oxytone (actriz, amor, atril, elasticidad, también). Thus vowel-final with penultimate stress, on the one hand, and consonant-final with final stress, on the other, are considered the unmarked stress patterns in Spanish.

new_statements.relation_note: Same generalization as the existing Baković 2016 statement (V-final penult, C-final final, lexical exceptions both ways, three-syllable window); adds the explicit contrastive-function statement, the verb/non-verb split (verbs predictable from morphology), secondary stress, the clitic escape from the window, and the plural stress shifts.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive ('función fonológica distintiva': sábana/sabana, crítica/critica, cantara/cantará) and only partially free: it must fall on one of the last three syllables. Non-verbs default to penultimate stress when vowel-final and final stress when consonant-final (unmarked patterns, computed on the singular without the number suffix), with 'numerous' lexical exceptions in both directions and a marked antepenultimate class; § 9.2b says morphological and segmental information is not sufficient to determine stress in nouns, adjectives and adverbs. Verb stress is morphologically determined and predictable (§ 9.1q; Morfología § 4.8a). Antepenultimate (esdrújula) is the most marked pattern, mostly vowel-final; consonant-final proparoxytones are a few learned words (déficit, régimen), names (Álvarez), Greek -sis loans and miércoles.
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 9.1z: secondary stresses exist, on syllables with less prominence than the lexically stressed one (bienvenido: primary on ni, secondary on bien, ve and do unstressed); § 9.2b: every stressed word has a single intensity stress, except some compounds and emphatic 'supplementary' stress; Morfología § 4.8a: the final tonal rise on enclitics (¿Dígame?) is sometimes interpreted as secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: § 9.4b/9.4f: vowel-final oxytones (bisturí, café, jabalí, mamá, menú, sofá, ojalá), consonant-final paroxytones (cónsul, difícil, lápiz, tórax, carácter, débil, huésped, joven, lunes, origen, útil, viernes, volumen; patronymics López, Márquez, Núñez; Greek names Aristides, Ulises), proparoxytones (árabe, época, romántico, título); final-diphthong words are oxytone (buey, convoy, virrey) except recent loans vóley, yérsey, yóquey, Sídney; regional doublets cóctel/coctel, chófer/chofer; § 9.1o: verb+clitic groups (cantándomelo, cómetelo) escape the three-syllable window because clitics do not count; § 9.4d-e: plural and gender inflection shift the pattern (crimen/crímenes, caimán/caimanes) and a few nouns shift the stress itself (régimen/regímenes, espécimen/especímenes, carácter/caracteres).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (sábana ~ sabana, crítica ~ critica, cantara ~ cantará) and restricted to one of the last three syllables (three-syllable window, breached only by verb+clitic forms like cómetelo). For nouns/adjectives/adverbs the unmarked patterns are penult stress in vowel-final words and final stress in consonant-final words (63.6% + 27% of stressed words in a 91,000-word corpus, together just over 90%); antepenult stress is marginal (~8%) and blocked when the penult is closed or has a diphthong. § 9.1m: some authors treat stress as 'mixed', predictable in some cases and 'impredecible.. de naturaleza léxica' in others; § 9.2b: morphological and segmental characterization is not sufficient to determine stress in non-verbal categories. Verbal stress (§ 9.6a-b) is morphologically determined and 'totalmente predecible': mostly penult (canto, cantaron), final in cantó/cantará, antepenult only in weak forms (cantábamos).
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 9.1r: 'En español, el acento secundario es asignado después del acento primario. Suele aparecer en sílabas alternas (PIES BINARIOS) a partir del acento primario y en dirección a las sílabas pretónicas: nàcionál, naciònalìzación, naciònalísmo, naciònalsòcialísmo. También puede encontrarse el acento secundario en la sílaba inicial de la palabra.. un fenómeno frecuente en ciertos estilos enfáticos de habla. Las palabras esdrújulas presentan en ocasiones un acento secundario en la sílaba final: últimò, párpadò.' No two adjacent stresses inside the word except -mente adverbs and some compounds (§ 9.5). Phonetic cue: F0 primarily, duration in Argentina (§ 9.1t).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-final oxytones, mostly loans (bisturí, café, sofá, ojalá, mamá; § 9.4b, 9.4l); consonant-final paroxytones (cónsul, difícil, lápiz, carácter, joven, patronymics López; § 9.4b, 9.4f); antepenult stress in learned/loan words (cálido, película, sábana, páprika; § 9.1ñ, 9.4g) and, with a closed penult, only Frómista, Mánchester, Ámsterdam (§ 9.4h); falling-diphthong-final words are oxytone (buey, virrey) except vóley, yérsey, yóquey, Sídney (§ 9.4f); stress shift in plurals régimen/regímenes, carácter/caracteres (§ 9.4e); verb+clitic superproparoxytones cómetelo (§ 9.1o); regional variation in loans cóctel ~ coctel, chófer ~ chofer (§ 9.4b, 9.4o-y).
new_statements.identity_note: The RAE/ASALE grammar describes pan-Hispanic standard Spanish and notes only peripheral regional facts for stress: duration as the main accentual cue in much of Argentina (§ 9.1t), voseo forms like cantás with final stress (§ 9.6a), and loanword variants cóctel ~ coctel, chófer ~ chofer across regions (§ 9.4b). No dialect-specific placement rule.

new_statements.quote: Evidence for the representation of the trill as an underlying cluster of taps comes from a restriction on stress assignment. Harris (1983) observes that in Spanish, when a penultimate syllable is closed by a consonant or a glide, stress cannot be assigned to the antepenultimate syllable. Accordingly, a native speaker would accept the nonce words mulangá or mulánga, but not *múlanga. The fact that native informants judge both nonce tamárro and tamarró to be possible but not *támarro is problematic for an analysis in which the surface trill is singly-linked to an underlying trill.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No general placement rule is stated (the thesis is about rhotics). It reports, following Harris 1983, one constraint on Spanish stress: antepenultimate stress is impossible when the penult is closed by a consonant or glide, while final and penultimate stress on the same nonce word are both acceptable (mulangá / mulánga), i.e. stress is not predictable within the right-edge window but the antepenult option is weight-restricted; words with an intervocalic trill in the last syllable are never proparoxytones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Not a grammar (the 'grammar sketch' tag is wrong: it is a psycholinguistic/computational thesis on lexicon structure built on a Spanish speech corpus). It states, in passing, that Spanish word stress is contrastive and not predictable from segmental information, that it is independent of syllable weight, and that the penultimate syllable is the statistically dominant position (only about 10% of the 324 frequent CVCV words in the Marcos Marín corpus are final-stressed; p. 72 calls first-syllable stress in disyllables 'most common, unmarked stress in Spanish'). Appendix C (p. 253) lists the 31 final-stressed CVCV words: 74% verbs, 16% nouns, 6% proper nouns, 3% adverbs, i.e. final stress in CVCV words is mostly verbal morphology (pasó etc.). The thesis also notes (p. 154) that infinitives carry stressed -ar/-er/-ir and that the stressed final vowel encodes verb tense and person.
new_statements.exceptions: No rule stated, so no exception classes; it only gives the corpus proportion (about 10% of frequent CVCV words final-stressed, mostly verb forms) and the observation that stress must be marked lexically (orthographic acute) and that stressed-vowel identity in final position is morphologically informative.

readall_conflicts: No placement disagreement among the three sources that speak to it (RAE 2011, Kireva 2016, Ortega-Llebaria & Prieto 2011) or with the catalog's existing Baković 2016 statement. The only difference is descriptive framing: Kireva (following Hualde 2005) states the non-verb default as weight-sensitive ('ultimate syllable.. if it is heavy, otherwise the penultimate'), whereas the RAE states it as ending-conditioned ('palabras terminadas en vocal son llanas.. acabadas en consonante suelen ser agudas') and adds that morphological and segmental information is not sufficient to determine non-verb stress (§ 9.2b); both describe the same surface generalization with the same exception classes (café, lápiz, régimen), so the reading remains lexical within a right-edge three-syllable window with defaults. The RAE also separates verbs, whose stress it calls morphologically determined and predictable (§ 9.1q), from non-verbs, which is compatible with Baković and with Kireva's footnotes. Five works could not be opened (UNM PDF behind an automated-access block, De Gruyter bot wall and wrong WALS record for Roca 1999, archive.org lending-only for Harris 1983, IPv6-only host for the ISSP proceedings) and the two opened prosody papers (Enbe & Tobin, Napoleão de Souza abstract) are silent on placement.

sources.quote: Evidence for the representation of the trill as an underlying cluster of taps comes from a restriction on stress assignment. Harris (1983) observes that in Spanish, when a penultimate syllable is closed by a consonant or a glide, stress cannot be assigned to the antepenultimate syllable. sources.quote: Unlike Catalan, there is no phonological vowel reduction in Castilian Spanish. Speakers produce the same five vocalic phonemes in stressed and unstressed positions.
